segments.text: How Do You Fix Voyager 1 From 24 Billion Kilometers Away?
In 1977, humanity sent a spacecraft called Voyager 1 to Jupiter and Saturn.
After completing its mission, it kept traveling, becoming the most distant operating spacecraft ever built by humans.
Decades later, in November 2023, its messages stopped making sense back on Earth.
The radio signal was still coming through.
The spacecraft was still receiving commands.
But neither its scientific measurements nor the information about its own condition could be read anymore.
How do you figure out what's broken when a spacecraft can't even tell you what's happening inside it?
By then, Voyager 1 was about 24 billion kilometers from Earth.
In 2012, it had crossed the boundary of the heliosphere — the enormous region around the Sun shaped by the solar wind and magnetic field.
Beyond that boundary, it had begun studying interstellar space.
There was no way to reach it and replace a part.
Radio communication was the only option.
But even that required patience.
A command sent from Earth took about twenty-two and a half hours to reach Voyager.
The reply took just as long to return.
To find out whether a single attempt had worked, engineers had to wait almost two days.
They spent months searching for the cause.
Their suspicions turned to one of the onboard computers.
It collected scientific and engineering data and prepared that information to be sent back to Earth.
In March 2024, the team sent a diagnostic command.
Once again, unusual data came back.
But this time, the engineers managed to decode it.
It was the contents of the onboard computer's memory.
By comparing it with earlier records, they found the problem.
About three percent of the memory had been damaged.
That section contained part of the program needed to prepare the spacecraft's messages.
They couldn't repair the chip onboard.
But they could try moving the necessary instructions into undamaged memory.
Then they ran into another problem.
No single free section of memory was large enough to hold that part of the program in one piece.
So the engineers split the code into smaller pieces and placed them in different locations.
Then they had to change the references inside the program, so the computer could find the instructions at their new addresses and all the pieces could work together again.
They decided to start with the program that prepared information about the spacecraft's condition.
If they could restore even that, the team would once again be able to see how its systems were working.
On April 18, they sent the fix from Earth.
It took almost a full day to reach Voyager.
Then the reply took almost another day to return.
On April 20, engineers received a message they could actually read.
For the first time in five months, the spacecraft had sent back understandable information about the condition of its systems.
Now they could turn to the scientific measurements.
By June, data was once again arriving from all four instruments that were still operating onboard at the time.
The damaged memory remained damaged.
But the engineers had found a way around it.
And a spacecraft launched almost half a century earlier could continue sending back scientific data from tens of billions of kilometers away.
